name: Edwardian, Georgian and Modernist Period (1901–1945)
description: Literature written in British, Irish and American English between the death of Queen Victoria and the end of the Second World War. The period opens with the Edwardian country-house novel and the Georgian anthology lyric, is broken open by the First World War and by the modernist experiments of 1910–1922 — free verse, the stream of consciousness, the mythical method, the little magazine — and closes with the politicised writing of the thirties and the literature of the Second World War. On the British and Irish side: Conrad, Ford, Forster, Lawrence, Joyce, Woolf and Richardson in prose; Yeats, Eliot, Pound, H.D. and the war poets in verse; Synge, O'Casey and the Abbey Theatre on the stage; and the Auden generation, Orwell, Huxley and Waugh in the thirties. On the American side: the expatriate modernism of Eliot, Pound and Stein; Frost, Stevens, Williams and Cummings; the Harlem Renaissance; the Lost Generation of Fitzgerald, Hemingway and Dos Passos; Faulkner and the Southern Renaissance; and the proletarian and documentary writing of the Depression.
historical_context: The period opens with the death of Victoria (January 1901) and the Edwardian interlude, and is dominated by two world wars. Between them: the coronation of Edward VII (1902) and the Entente Cordiale (1904); the great Liberal landslide of 1906 and the 'People's Budget' of 1909; the Parliament Act of 1911 and the Irish Home Rule crisis; the militant suffrage campaign from 1905 and the Cat and Mouse Act of 1913; the First World War (1914–18) with its conscription acts, its censorship and its ten million dead; the Easter Rising (1916) and the Anglo-Irish War (1919–21), the treaty of 1921 and the Free State of 1922; the Representation of the People Act (1918) enfranchising women over thirty; the General Strike (1926) and the Great Depression after 1929; the rise of fascism and the Spanish Civil War (1936–39); and the Second World War (1939–45) with the Blitz and the Holocaust. In the United States: the Progressive era and the First World War; Prohibition (1920–33) and the Jazz Age; the Great Migration of African Americans northward; the Harlem Renaissance; the crash of 1929 and the New Deal; and entry into the Second World War in 1941. Technologically: the motor car, the aeroplane, the telephone, wireless broadcasting from 1922, the cinema and the cheap newspaper transformed the conditions of writing and of reading.
literary_characteristics: A literature of formal rupture and of violent historical pressure. Verse abandons the iambic contract for free verse, the image, the fragment and the collage; the long poem becomes a structure of quotation and myth rather than of narrative, from The Waste Land (1922) to The Bridge (1930) and Four Quartets (1943). Prose fiction turns inward to consciousness and outward to documentary: the stream of consciousness of Richardson, Joyce, Woolf and Faulkner on one side, the reportage, the proletarian novel and the Mass Observation survey on the other. Drama is reinvented by the Irish movement, by the problem play and by the verse drama of the thirties. Criticism becomes an academic discipline and a modernist instrument at once (Eliot, Richards, Empson, Leavis), and the little magazine — Blast, The Egoist, The Little Review, The Criterion, transition — becomes the period's characteristic institution. The popular genres of the period, the detective novel, the ghost story and the scientific romance, are among its most durable achievements.
